Story: The Iron Gate Descends (dark fantasy)

Premise: A Durnish knight, clad in heavy blackened plate, stands at the threshold of the goblin caves beneath the Ashen Spire, having just forced open an iron gate. The prince’s signet ring, discovered in the mud, confirms his passage into the tunnels. The air is thick with the scent of damp earth and the faint glow of fungi, while the distant sound of movement hints at unseen dangers ahead. The Church’s decree to retrieve the prince or die trying weighs heavily, but the immediate threat is the darkness itself.

The player is in Iron Gate Chamber: The iron gate lies half-buried in the stone floor, its jagged teeth glinting dully in the pale glow of bioluminescent fungi clinging to the cavern walls. The air is thick with the scent of damp earth and rust, the taste of iron sharp on your tongue. The tunnel ahead yawns black and slick with moisture, the faint sound of skittering claws echoing from its depths. Your boot sinks slightly into the muddy threshold, where a single, deep groove cuts across the stone—fresh, as if something heavy was dragged through. The dim light flickers, casting long, wavering shadows that seem to crawl along the obsidian walls.

Ways out of here: tunnel upward, obsidian maw. There are no others.

The player is Veythra the Silent.

Veythra the Silent is unhurt.

The story has ended: The cell is opened and the prince is already cold; the decree is answered, and not the way anybody wanted.

Nobody else is here.

Lying here, and takeable: iron key.

The player is carrying: prince's signet ring.

What just happened: ON THIS TURN, and not before it, Veythra the Silent picked the prince's signet ring up. Until this turn it was NOT in their hands at all: it was lying in Iron Gate Chamber. Now they are carrying it -- A heavy gold ring, its surface etched with the royal crest of Durnhold, still caked with mud. The metal is cold and slightly bent, as if wrenched from a finger.. The picking up is what has just happened and it is what to narrate. Do not write it as something they already had, already held, or turn out to be holding. The prince's signet ring is the only thing that moved: nothing else was lifted, opened, drawn out or taken into anybody's hands.

Earlier, in order:
The player steps into the Iron Gate Chamber, encountering the sensory overload of the cavern’s atmosphere and the immediate presence of the tunnel ahead.
[generated prelude summary]

Write the ending.

prelude.description: You crouch, fingers brushing the mud-caked metal, and lift the prince's signet ring from the groove in the stone. The weight of it is solid, the gold cold and slightly bent, as if torn from a finger in haste. The royal crest of Durnhold glints dully in the dim fungal light, the mud clinging to its etched surface. It fits snugly in your palm, a silent testament to the prince’s passage—and the Church’s decree now pressed into your grip. The tunnel ahead still yawns, the skittering sounds unchanged, but the ring is yours now, heavy with purpose.

Premise: The player is a ward clerk in Ambry who finds an hour cut out of their own daybook and the desk opposite theirs cleared of a colleague they can no longer quite remember. Working out what happened in that hour means going through the Registry's own paperwork against it: the supply closet nobody has inventoried, the long hallway with the Inspectorate coming up it, and eventually the question of who has blank writs and why one was spent on a Marginalia clerk in Ward Office 12. The tone is dry, close and procedural, and the horror is entirely administrative.

The player is in Ward Office 12: You are standing at your own desk on the second floor of the Registry's east ring, in a room built for four clerks and staffed, lately, by two. The gas mantle above the desks is turned low and hissing. Rain comes off the levee and goes sideways past the window, and the glass is cold enough to feel from here. Your daybook lies open under your hand with the stamp beside it, and the ruled gap between four and five o'clock sits in the middle of the page looking exactly as legitimate as every other line on it.

The desk across from yours has been cleared to the wood -- no blotter, no cylinder, no apron over the chair back -- and the chair is squared to the desk the way nobody ever leaves a chair they intend to come back to. On the wall between the windows, the pneumatic tube gapes open with no carrier in it. The door to the long hallway stands ajar on the darkening corridor, and beside the filing press, half-hidden by the coat rail, is the narrow door of the supply closet: no inventory number, no audit slip, no lock. Somewhere down the hallway a door closes, nearer than the last one.

Ways out of here: The Supply Closet, The Long Hallway. There are no others.

Story: The Unrecorded Hour (bureaucratic mystery)

Premise: The player is a ward clerk in Ambry who finds an hour cut out of their own daybook and the desk opposite theirs cleared of a colleague they can no longer quite remember. Working out what happened in that hour means going through the Registry's own paperwork against it: the supply closet nobody has inventoried, the long hallway with the Inspectorate coming up it, and eventually the question of who has blank writs and why one was spent on a Marginalia clerk in Ward Office 12. The tone is dry, close and procedural, and the horror is entirely administrative.

The player is in Ward Office 12: You are standing at your own desk on the second floor of the Registry's east ring, in a room built for four clerks and staffed, lately, by two. The gas mantle above the desks is turned low and hissing. Rain comes off the levee and goes sideways past the window, and the glass is cold enough to feel from here. Your daybook lies open under your hand with the stamp beside it, and the ruled gap between four and five o'clock sits in the middle of the page looking exactly as legitimate as every other line on it.

The desk across from yours has been cleared to the wood -- no blotter, no cylinder, no apron over the chair back -- and the chair is squared to the desk the way nobody ever leaves a chair they intend to come back to. On the wall between the windows, the pneumatic tube gapes open with no carrier in it. The door to the long hallway stands ajar on the darkening corridor, and beside the filing press, half-hidden by the coat rail, is the narrow door of the supply closet: no inventory number, no audit slip, no lock. Somewhere down the hallway a door closes, nearer than the last one.

Ways out of here: The Supply Closet, The Long Hallway. There are no others.

Beneath it, the scrape of stone on stone, slow and deliberate, as if something is dragging itself just beyond the edge of the light. Then, a whisper of breath, shallow and uneven, from the far corner where the prince sits. His fingers twitch against the stone, but he does not speak. The chain on the floor shivers, though no wind stirs it.

readings.prompt:
Story: The Unrecorded Hour (bureaucratic mystery)

Premise: The player is a ward clerk in Ambry who finds an hour cut out of their own daybook and the desk opposite theirs cleared of a colleague they can no longer quite remember. Working out what happened in that hour means going through the Registry's own paperwork against it: the supply closet nobody has inventoried, the long hallway with the Inspectorate coming up it, and eventually the question of who has blank writs and why one was spent on a Marginalia clerk in Ward Office 12. The tone is dry, close and procedural, and the horror is entirely administrative.

The player is in Ward Office 12: You are standing at your own desk on the second floor of the Registry's east ring, in a room built for four clerks and staffed, lately, by two. The gas mantle above the desks is turned low and hissing. Rain comes off the levee and goes sideways past the window, and the glass is cold enough to feel from here. Your daybook lies open under your hand with the stamp beside it, and the ruled gap between four and five o'clock sits in the middle of the page looking exactly as legitimate as every other line on it.

The desk across from yours has been cleared to the wood -- no blotter, no cylinder, no apron over the chair back -- and the chair is squared to the desk the way nobody ever leaves a chair they intend to come back to. On the wall between the windows, the pneumatic tube gapes open with no carrier in it. The door to the long hallway stands ajar on the darkening corridor, and beside the filing press, half-hidden by the coat rail, is the narrow door of the supply closet: no inventory number, no audit slip, no lock. Somewhere down the hallway a door closes, nearer than the last one.

Ways out of here: The Supply Closet, The Long Hallway. There are no others.

The player is Odile Vance.

Odile Vance is unhurt.

The story has ended: With Perrin's index and the unsigned writ side by side on your desk, the missing hour has a source at last -- the same hand closed 0714, 0902 and Perrin Lasco. Query 1188 stays open in your name, and this time the record says why.

Nobody else is here.

Dead here: Halkett Rowe (Sub-Inspector Rowe). They cannot speak or act.

Lying here, and takeable: filing press, ward stamp, Inspectorate seal, grey coat, shoes.

The player is carrying: Ward Office 12 daybook, spectacles, blank closure writ, Perrin's private index.

The player is wearing: office coat.

What just happened: ON THIS TURN, and not before it, Odile Vance picked the blank closure writ up. Until this turn it was NOT in their hands at all: it was lying in Ward Office 12. Now they are carrying it -- A Registry writ of closure on the heavy grey stock only the Inspectorate issues, lying in the wire basket under the pneumatic tube where it arrived without a carrier. It is ward-marked 12, sealed, and countersigned in advance; the line for the name of the file to be closed is still empty, and the countersignature is in the same careful, borrowed slant as the amendment in your daybook.. The picking up is what has just happened and it is what to narrate. Do not write it as something they already had, already held, or turn out to be holding. The blank closure writ is the only thing that moved: nothing else was lifted, opened, drawn out or taken into anybody's hands. This is exactly what is written on it, word for word: "WRIT OF CLOSURE — Ward 12. The file of ______________________ is closed, no query to be raised. By order of the Inspectorate. Countersigned." -- those are the words on it, and they do not change between readings. Quote them as they are; do not add to them, and do not write different ones.

Earlier, in order:
The story opens in Ward Office 12 with Sub-Inspector Rowe arriving forty minutes early, the missing hour still open on the daybook, and the uninventoried supply closet at the player's back.
A fight in Ward Office 12: 1 blow over 1 round. Halkett Rowe is dead.
You reach into the wire basket beneath the pneumatic tube and lift out the blank closure writ.

Write the ending.

readings.prompt:
Story: The Unrecorded Hour (bureaucratic mystery)

Premise: The player is a ward clerk in Ambry who finds an hour cut out of their own daybook and the desk opposite theirs cleared of a colleague they can no longer quite remember. Working out what happened in that hour means going through the Registry's own paperwork against it: the supply closet nobody has inventoried, the long hallway with the Inspectorate coming up it, and eventually the question of who has blank writs and why one was spent on a Marginalia clerk in Ward Office 12. The tone is dry, close and procedural, and the horror is entirely administrative.

The player is in Ward Office 12: You are standing at your own desk on the second floor of the Registry's east ring, in a room built for four clerks and staffed, lately, by two. The gas mantle above the desks is turned low and hissing. Rain comes off the levee and goes sideways past the window, and the glass is cold enough to feel from here. Your daybook lies open under your hand with the stamp beside it, and the ruled gap between four and five o'clock sits in the middle of the page looking exactly as legitimate as every other line on it.

The desk across from yours has been cleared to the wood -- no blotter, no cylinder, no apron over the chair back -- and the chair is squared to the desk the way nobody ever leaves a chair they intend to come back to. On the wall between the windows, the pneumatic tube gapes open with no carrier in it. The door to the long hallway stands ajar on the darkening corridor, and beside the filing press, half-hidden by the coat rail, is the narrow door of the supply closet: no inventory number, no audit slip, no lock. Somewhere down the hallway a door closes, nearer than the last one.

Ways out of here: The Supply Closet, The Long Hallway. There are no others.

The player is Odile Vance.

Odile Vance is unhurt.

The story has ended: With Perrin's index and the unsigned writ side by side on your desk, the missing hour has a source at last -- the same hand closed 0714, 0902 and Perrin Lasco. Query 1188 stays open in your name, and this time the record says why.

Nobody else is here.

Dead here: Halkett Rowe (Sub-Inspector Rowe). They cannot speak or act.

Lying here, and takeable: filing press, ward stamp, Inspectorate seal, grey coat, shoes.

The player is carrying: Ward Office 12 daybook, spectacles, blank closure writ, Perrin's private index.

The player is wearing: office coat.

Now they are carrying it -- A Registry writ of closure on the heavy grey stock only the Inspectorate issues, lying in the wire basket under the pneumatic tube where it arrived without a carrier. It is ward-marked 12, sealed, and countersigned in advance; the line for the name of the file to be closed is still empty, and the countersignature is in the same careful, borrowed slant as the amendment in your daybook..
